title: Spiders Sleep Like Us? 5 Animals That Sleep in Impossible Ways
description: A new study filmed jumping spiders sleeping in two stages, with twitching legs and flickering eyes, just like REM sleep. We count down five animals that sleep in impossible ways: penguins that nap 10,000 times a day, dolphins that sleep with half a brain, birds that sleep in flight, seals that sleep while sinking, and the spiders that might dream.

scenes.say: A spider in a lab just did something only dreamers do. Its eyes twitched in its sleep.

scenes.label: New study
scenes.say: Okay, so that's not a joke. A study published this week filmed it on infrared cameras, night after night.

scenes.label: Do they dream?
scenes.say: And it raises a question nobody expected. Do spiders actually dream? We'll get to that at the very end.
But first, you need to see how strange sleep really is. Because some animals sleep in ways that sound impossible.

scenes.label: 5 strange sleepers
scenes.say: Today, five animals that sleep in the weirdest ways on Earth. Each one stranger than the last.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: And stay for number one. It's the animal hanging in the corner of your room right now.

scenes.label: 10,000 naps a day
scenes.say: Number five. The penguin that naps more than ten thousand times a day. And you'll see why.
Chinstrap penguins nest in huge, noisy colonies in Antarctica. Some colonies hold hundreds of thousands of birds.

scenes.label: Brainwave sensors
scenes.say: Scientists wanted to know how they sleep in all that chaos. So they used EEG, the same brainwave recording doctors use on people.
Here's what they found. These penguins don't really sleep at night. They take microsleeps. Tiny naps, all day long.

scenes.label: About 4 seconds
scenes.say: How tiny? About four seconds each. Close your eyes, count to four, and you're done. That's a whole nap.

scenes.label: 10,000+ per day
scenes.say: And they do it more than ten thousand times a day. Ten thousand little naps.

scenes.label: 11+ hours total
scenes.say: Now here's the wild part. Add them all up, and they get over eleven hours of sleep a day.
So why sleep like that? Think about their life. One parent feeds at sea for days. The other one guards the eggs alone.
Predators and other penguins are always nearby. A long, deep sleep could be dangerous. So they sleep in blinks.
Scientists called it one of the most extreme examples of sleep adding up, a little at a time. Imagine living like that.

scenes.label: Half a brain asleep
scenes.say: Number four. The animal that sleeps with half its brain, while the other half keeps watch.
Dolphins have a problem you don't have. They breathe air, but they live underwater. So if they fully pass out, they could drown.
Back in 1964, a scientist noticed something odd. Resting dolphins kept only one eye closed.

scenes.label: One half sleeps
scenes.say: Later, researchers recorded their brainwaves. Usually, one half of the brain was in deep sleep. The other half was awake.

scenes.label: Sleeping half cools
scenes.say: And here's a weird detail. The sleeping half actually cooled down. The awake half kept the same temperature.
Meanwhile, the awake half keeps swimming, and brings the dolphin up to the surface to breathe.

scenes.label: Eye on the pod
scenes.say: And that open eye? It often watches the other dolphins in the pod. If a buddy swims to the other side, the dolphin switches eyes.

scenes.label: 2/3 awake
scenes.say: Bottlenose dolphins spend almost two thirds of the day awake. The rest is half-brain sleep.

scenes.label: Sentinel ducks
scenes.say: And they're not alone. Ducks do it too. Ducks on the edge of a group sleep with one eye open, facing outward.
In one study, those edge ducks had about one hundred fifty percent more half-brain sleep than ducks in the middle.
But dolphins sleep in the water. What about an animal that sleeps in the sky? Because that's next.

scenes.label: Sleeps in the air
scenes.say: Number three. The bird that falls asleep while it's flying, high over the ocean.
This is the great frigatebird. A big seabird that can stay up in the air for days at a time.

scenes.label: Galápagos
scenes.say: In the Galápagos Islands, scientists fitted these birds with tiny brainwave recorders and GPS trackers.

scenes.label: 10 days nonstop
scenes.say: Then the birds took off. Some flew nonstop for up to ten days, covering three thousand kilometers.

scenes.label: Asleep mid-flight
scenes.say: So when do they sleep? The answer surprised everyone. They sleep in the air, while gliding.
Often with one half of the brain, just like dolphins. And the eye facing the turn usually stayed awake.

scenes.label: 42 minutes a day
scenes.say: But here's the twist. In the air, they slept only about forty two minutes a day. Total.

scenes.label: 12+ hours on land
scenes.say: Back on land, the same birds slept over twelve hours a day. Deeper and longer. They were catching up.
And their dream-like REM sleep in the air? It lasted only a few seconds at a time. Just seconds.
Think about that. Ten days in the sky, on less than an hour of sleep a day. And they still fly just fine.

scenes.label: Subscribe
scenes.say: Quick thing. If you like secrets like this, subscribe. One animal secret a day, and number one is coming.

scenes.label: Sleeps while sinking
scenes.say: Number two. The seal that falls asleep while sinking into the dark.

scenes.label: 2+ tons
scenes.say: Northern elephant seals are huge. Adult males can weigh more than two tons.

scenes.label: 90% underwater
scenes.say: They spend months at sea, and about ninety percent of that time they're underwater.

scenes.label: Sleep cap
scenes.say: Nobody knew how they slept out there. So a scientist named Jessica Kendall-Bar built a waterproof sleep cap. She tested it on herself first.
Then the team put it on wild seals in California, with the same kind of electrodes used in human sleep clinics.

scenes.label: Dive, then sleep
scenes.say: Okay, so here's what happens. A seal dives down. And as it sinks, it falls asleep.

scenes.label: REM after ~1 min
scenes.say: After about a minute, it enters REM sleep. Its muscles go loose. And it starts to spin.

scenes.label: Falling-leaf spiral
scenes.say: It flips upside down and spirals down like a falling leaf. Hundreds of feet. Fast asleep.
Why so deep? Deep water is dark. Predators are more of a problem near the surface. So down there is safer.

scenes.label: ~2 hours a day
scenes.say: Each nap lasts roughly five to ten minutes. And at sea, they sleep only about two hours a day. For months.

scenes.label: 14 hours on land
scenes.say: That rivals African elephants for the least sleep of any mammal. Then back on land, they sleep up to fourteen hours a day.

scenes.label: Fatigued Fiona
scenes.say: One seal, nicknamed Fatigued Fiona, even finished her nap lying on the seafloor. I love that.
So a penguin naps in seconds, and a seal naps while sinking. But none of them can do what number one did this week.

scenes.label: Spiders sleep like us
scenes.say: Number one. The spiders that sleep like us. And might even dream.

scenes.label: See-through babies
scenes.say: This story started back in 2022. Baby jumping spiders have see-through bodies. So scientists could look inside their heads.

scenes.label: Moving retinas
scenes.say: Jumping spiders can't roll their eyes like you. But inside, their tube-shaped retinas can move. And at night, they did.

scenes.label: Twitching legs
scenes.say: And every time the eyes moved, the legs curled in and twitched. A lot like a dog running in its sleep.

scenes.label: Bonn, Oct 2026
scenes.say: Now here's the new study. Published on October 27, 2026, in PNAS, by a team at the University of Bonn.

scenes.label: Up to 10 mm
scenes.say: Their spider is Portia fimbriata, a jumping spider from northern Australia. Up to ten millimeters long.

scenes.label: Upside down
scenes.say: At night, it hangs upside down in a small web. And the team filmed them all night with infrared cameras.

scenes.label: Stage 1: still
scenes.say: Here's what they saw. First, the spider cleans itself. Then it slowly goes still. That's one stage.

scenes.label: Stage 2: REM-like
scenes.say: Then comes a second stage. Eye flickers, legs curling, little twitches. A REM-like stage.

scenes.label: The noise test
scenes.say: But how do you prove it's sleep and not just resting? The team played a loud noise and timed how fast the spiders reacted.

scenes.label: Some never woke
scenes.say: In both stages, they reacted slower. Slowest in the twitching stage. Some didn't react at all. That's what sleep looks like.
One spider expert called it the most complete case for sleep in any arachnid. Ever.

scenes.label: ~500 million years
scenes.say: And the bigger idea? Spiders and animals like us split apart roughly five hundred million years ago.
So if a spider's tiny brain sleeps in two stages, sleep may be far older than we thought. That's what the lead scientist said.

scenes.label: Nobody knows yet
scenes.say: So, do spiders dream? Honestly, nobody knows yet. Their brain activity wasn't even measured. Only their behavior.

scenes.label: Dreams of vibrations?
scenes.say: But here's my favorite thought. One researcher said a spider's dream, if it has one, might not be pictures. It could be vibrations.
So tonight, that little spider in the corner might be twitching. Maybe dreaming of a web that shakes.
Ten thousand naps. Half a brain. Sleeping in the sky. Spiraling down asleep. And a twitching spider.

scenes.label: Your vote?
scenes.say: So, which one surprised you most? And do you think spiders dream? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: Spiders Sleep Like Us. Scientists Just Filmed It
short.description: A new study filmed jumping spiders sleeping in two stages, with REM-like twitches. Do they dream? Full countdown of the strangest sleepers on my channel.

scenes.say: Scientists just caught spiders sleeping like us. Twitching legs, flickering eyes, two stages a night.
This week, a University of Bonn team filmed Australian jumping spiders hanging upside down in their webs all night.
First, the spider cleans itself and goes still. Then the legs curl, the eyes flicker, and little twitches start.
They played a loud noise. Sleeping spiders reacted slower, slowest while twitching. Some never reacted at all.
Spiders split from animals like us about five hundred million years ago. So sleep might be ancient.
Do they dream? Nobody knows. But one researcher thinks it might feel like vibrations.
So tonight, the spider in your corner might be twitching, because scientists just caught spiders sleeping like us.
